sections.b: The book of Lamentations is the Bible's longest sustained lament. Chapters 1 and 2 mourn the city as a woman, chapter 3 is a man's lament that turns in the middle to trust, chapter 4 compares the city's gold with its clay, and chapter 5 is the community's prayer. Complaint and confession stand together throughout (1:18, 20; 3:42; 5:16), and the book ends without an answer (5:22).

Lamentations does not choose between saying that Jerusalem suffers because she sinned (1:8; 3:39; 5:16) and saying that the suffering is out of proportion and that God has acted like an enemy (2:4-5; 3:1-18). Chapter 3 asks why a living person should complain about his sins (3:39) just after it says that God does not afflict from his heart (3:33).

The book describes the fall of Jerusalem in the words of the covenant curses (Deuteronomy 28:49-57; Leviticus 26): a siege, hunger so great that parents eat their children (Lamentations 2:20; 4:10), no rest among the nations (1:3), and the enemy as head (1:5). It says plainly that the LORD did it (2:17). It also asks whether it was fair (2:20; 5:7).
sections.refs: Lamentations 1:3; Lamentations 1:5; Lamentations 2:17; Lamentations 2:20; Lamentations 4:10; Deuteronomy 28:49-57

sections.b: Lamentations uses many Hebrew words for God's anger: 'af, charon 'af, chemah, 'evrah and za'am. Chapter 2 is a catalogue of what that anger does. The Plain gives each word its own English word. The book also says that God does not afflict "from his heart" (3:33) and that his anger does not last forever (3:31).

sections.h: Lamentations: the view from just after 586 BC
sections.b: Lamentations is the earliest poetry of the exile, written close to the event. It speaks of captivity (1:3, 5, 18; 2:14; 4:22), of wandering without rest, of exiles in Babylon and of the poor who remained (5:2-18). It ends with the hope that the exile will not be repeated (4:22) and a prayer to be brought back (5:21).

Lamentations 4:21-22 tells Edom to be glad while it can: the cup of God's anger will pass to it. The charge is the same as in Obadiah and Psalm 137:7, that Edom cheered and profited at Jerusalem's fall. The verse names "the land of Uz" as Edom's home. In later Jewish writing Edom stood for Rome.

Lamentations is the Bible's book of the ruined Jerusalem: its gates, streets and walls, its songs of Zion mocked (2:15), its priests and prophets killed in the sanctuary (2:20). It treats the city as the sufferer, a woman with a name, and not as a place.

The songs of Zion said that God would defend the city (Psalm 46; 48; 76). Lamentations says the kings of the earth believed it too (4:12) and records what happened. The last picture of the book is Mount Zion, desolate, with foxes on it (5:18), set beside the prayer that the LORD sits as king forever (5:19).

The poems describe the temple in ruins: strangers in the sanctuary (1:10), the altar thrown out and the sanctuary disowned (2:7), the festival forgotten (2:6), priests and prophets killed in the sanctuary (2:20). They say the LORD himself tore down his booth. They do not call for its rebuilding.

The best-known sentence of Lamentations puts hesed in the plural, "the LORD's acts of loyal love", at the turn of chapter 3, spoken by a man who has just said God is a bear, a lion and an archer. It comes from the creed of Exodus 34:6-7 and is paired with God's compassions and faithfulness (3:22-23). The same chapter says that God "will have compassion, as great as his acts of loyal love" (3:32).

sections.h: Compassions that do not run out
sections.b: Rachamim in Lamentations 3:22 and 3:32 comes from the word for "womb". The same root names the "compassionate" women of 4:10 who boiled their children, and the book sets the two uses of it side by side without comment.

Chapters 1, 2 and 4 of Lamentations give each verse one letter in order; chapter 3 gives each letter three verses; chapter 5 has 22 verses but no alphabet. In chapter 1 ayin comes before pe; in chapters 2, 3 and 4 pe comes first. Commentators read the form as completeness and order within disorder. Greek and Latin Bibles print the letter names before the verses.

In the Hebrew Bible Lamentations is in the Writings, among the Five Scrolls. In Greek, Latin and Protestant Bibles it follows Jeremiah, because the Greek and Latin preface and church tradition make Jeremiah its author; in Greek and Orthodox Bibles it comes after Baruch. The Letter of Jeremiah is Baruch 6 in the Latin Bible and a separate book in some Greek Bibles.

Tradition, from the Talmud and the Greek and Latin preface on, makes Jeremiah the author of Lamentations; most modern scholars doubt it. The two books share language ("terror all around", Lamentations 2:22; Jeremiah 6:25), images (weeping eyes, Lamentations 3:48; Jeremiah 9:1) and a charge against the false prophets (Lamentations 2:14; Jeremiah 23:16).

Lamentations 4:20 mourns the capture of "the LORD's anointed", "the breath of our nostrils". The commonest view is Zedekiah, caught near Jericho (2 Kings 25:4-7); Rashi takes the anointed to be Josiah. Christian readers have heard Christ in the Greek and Latin "Christ the Lord". The Plain keeps the Hebrew.
The captured anointed one of 4:20 is a Davidic king, not yet a future messiah. Later Jewish and Christian readers heard a messianic note in the Greek and Latin wording; the Hebrew states a loss.

sections.h: Fasts for the fall of Jerusalem
sections.b: Zechariah mentions fasts in the fifth and seventh months that the people kept for seventy years (Zechariah 7:3-5; 8:19). Jewish custom keeps the fast of the fifth month as the Ninth of Av, when Lamentations is read.

The Plain keeps Hebrew words for wrongdoing apart: pesha' "rebellion" (1:5, 14, 22; 3:42), chet "sin" (1:8; 3:39; 4:6, 13; 5:16), 'avon "guilt" (2:14; 4:6, 13, 22; 5:7) and marah "defy" (1:18, 20; 3:42). The book admits sin (1:5, 8, 18; 3:42; 5:16) and also asks whether children should bear it (5:7).
sections.refs: Lamentations 1:5; Lamentations 1:8; Lamentations 1:18; Lamentations 3:42; Lamentations 5:7; Lamentations 5:16

sections.b: The community says its ancestors sinned and are gone and that it carries their guilt (5:7), and then says "we have sinned" (5:16). Ezekiel 18:2-4 and Jeremiah 31:29-30 reject the saying that children's teeth are set on edge by their parents' sour grapes, but the Law and Kings speak of guilt that falls on later generations (Exodus 20:5; 2 Kings 23:26).
sections.refs: Lamentations 5:7; Lamentations 5:16; Ezekiel 18:2; Jeremiah 31:29; Exodus 20:5; 2 Kings 23:26

sections.b: In 3:40 the community says "let us return to the LORD"; in 5:21 it asks God to do the bringing back, "Bring us back to yourself, LORD, and we will come back." The same turning (Hebrew shuv) is both human act and divine gift, as in Jeremiah 31:18 and Psalm 80.

The poems are full of prayer: "See, LORD, and look" (1:9, 11, 20; 2:20), the call to cry out at night (2:18-19), the confession of 3:40-42, the prayer for repayment (3:64-66) and the community's prayer of chapter 5. The prayer of 3:55-57 recalls a time when God drew near and said "Do not be afraid".

Lamentations asks God to do to the enemies what he has done to the city (1:21-22) and ends chapter 3 with a prayer that he repay them, give them a covered heart and wipe them out from under the heavens (3:64-66). Like the curse psalms, the prayer leaves vengeance to God. Edom's cup (4:21-22) is the third such passage.
Lamentations 4:6 says Jerusalem's guilt was greater than Sodom's, since Sodom was overturned in a moment while Jerusalem starved for months. Ezekiel 16:48-50 also ranks Jerusalem's sin above Sodom's.

Lamentations plays on the festival (mo'ed): the pilgrim roads are empty (1:4), the LORD makes festival and Sabbath forgotten (2:6), he "calls a festival" against the young (1:15), and invites terrors as to a festival day (2:22).

Lamentations opens with Jerusalem "like a widow" (1:1) and later says that the people's mothers are "like widows" (5:3). A widow without sons had no income and no protector in Israel; the image makes the city's helplessness plain.

sections.h: Sexual violence in the sack of Jerusalem
sections.b: Lamentations speaks of the city as a woman stripped and seen naked by those who once honored her (1:8-10), and in 5:11 says plainly that women in Zion and young women in the towns of Judah were raped. The Hebrew verb is 'innu, the verb used of Dinah (Genesis 34:2) and Tamar (2 Samuel 13); the Plain says "raped" here because the verse stands alone in a list of things done to a conquered people. The book does not hide it, and does not blame the women.

"Good is the LORD to people who wait for him, to anyone who looks for him" (3:25) uses three Hebrew words for waiting and seeking (yachal, qavah, darash) and says it is good to wait in silence for the LORD's rescue (3:26).

sections.h: Good and troubles from one mouth (Lamentations 3:37-38)
sections.b: Lamentations 3:37-38 asks who has spoken and it came to be unless the Lord ordered it, and whether both troubles and good do not come from the Most High's mouth. Churches read it differently: as God's rule over all things (Reformed), as the hidden God (Lutheran), as God permitting evil (Catholic and Orthodox), or as not meaning that God decrees sin (Methodist). See the card at Lamentations 3.

The Chronicler says Jeremiah lamented Josiah and that the singers kept it in "the Laments" (2 Chronicles 35:25). The Talmud tells that Josiah, shot by Pharaoh's archers, said "The LORD is righteous" (Lamentations 1:18); Rashi takes "the LORD's anointed" in 4:20 to be Josiah. Most scholars do not think the book is Josiah's lament.
"he gave no thought to his footstool" (2:1) uses a word that the Bible attaches to the ark, the sanctuary and Zion (1 Chronicles 28:2; Psalm 132:7; Psalm 99:5). No view is settled for the verse.

Three infinitives name three wrongs: trampling prisoners, bending a person's rights and subverting a lawsuit. The last words ask whether the Lord does not see. They set the poet's complaint beside the Law's demand for fair courts.
The man in Lamentations 3 says God has made him drink wormwood (3:15), and asks God to remember it (3:19). The bitter plant is paired with "poison" as in Deuteronomy 29:18.

Lamentations shows nearly every curse of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 in action: no rest among the nations (1:3), the enemy as head (1:5), the sword outside and terror inside (1:20), and parents eating their children (2:20; 4:10).

Lamentations is the poetry of the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC. It names the famine (1:11; 4:4-10), the entry of foreigners into the sanctuary (1:10), the flight and capture of the king (4:19-20) and Edom's gloating (4:21-22). It does not give names, dates or numbers; for those see 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 39 and 52.

The commonest view of the LORD's anointed, trapped in their pits (Lamentations 4:20) is Zedekiah, who fled the city, was caught on the plains of Jericho and taken to Babylon (2 Kings 25:4-7). Others name Josiah or the Davidic king in general.
The book calls Judah's allies her "lovers" who betrayed her (1:2, 19), looks in vain for "a nation that does not save" (4:17), and remembers a hand given to Egypt and Assyria for bread (5:6).

Lamentations blames the prophets for visions that were "empty and false" and did not lay bare the people's guilt (2:14), and it names the sins of prophets and priests as the cause of the fall (4:13). It also says no vision comes from the LORD now (2:9).
In the same verse that the community says "we have rebelled and defied", it says to God "you have not forgiven". The book's last prayer asks God to bring them back (5:21).

Jerusalem becomes niddah, an "unclean thing" (1:8, 17); the blind priests and prophets are cried at with "Keep away, unclean!" (4:15). In both places the language of the purity laws is used for a people cut off from the sanctuary.
The poems repeat and answer the psalms: Psalm 74 and 79 on the temple destroyed, Psalm 88 and 69 on the pit, Psalm 137 on Edom, Psalm 143:3 in Lamentations 3:6 and Psalm 102:12 in Lamentations 5:19.

sections.b: The first four poems are alphabet poems in the limping lament measure; the fifth is the same length without the alphabet. The voices shift from narrator to city to man to community. Reading the book in order moves from a description of the ruin to a prayer.

sections.h: Lamentations and the Ninth of Av
sections.b: Lamentations is the scroll of the Ninth of Av. Jewish tradition reads it in the evening in a dim synagogue, in a low voice, and repeats 5:21 after 5:22. The reading follows the Jewish custom of fasting for the destruction of the temple.

Lamentations calls the city Daughter Zion, Daughter Judah, Daughter Jerusalem and, for Edom, Daughter Edom. The "daughter of my people" (2:11; 3:48; 4:3, 6, 10) is the people as a daughter. The city weeps (1:2), speaks (1:12-22), is told to cry out (2:18) and is comforted by no one.
Lamentations is the scroll of the Ninth of Av, the day the temple is mourned. It is the only one of the five read at a fast.

The book shares with Mesopotamian laments a mourning woman who is the city, a catalogue of destruction and a poet speaking for the city. It differs in naming its own God as the destroyer, in its confession of sin, and in having no scene of return.
